title: KV shim: lazy dequantization and low-copy execution path for mixed-precision kernels
content:
Purpose and scope:
This doc proposes a lightweight 'KV shim' layer that enables lazy dequantization and zero-copy handoff between the KV cache and mixed-precision execution kernels (INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ). Goal: reduce memory copies, lower peak GPU memory, and preserve deterministic outputs while keeping kernel implementations minimally invasive.

Motivation / problems we see today:
- Frequent dequantize->compute->requantize cycles cause extra GPU memory pressure and memory bandwidth tax for latency-sensitive single-request workloads.
- Mixed-precision kernels have different input encodings; the runtime currently forces an eager, global dequantize of KV shards to a canonical precision before dispatch. This is wasteful when many requests only need prefix KV access or when kernels can operate on quantized slices.
- Switching precision (fallbacks, canaries) forces full-copy conversion of the entire KV shard, blocking scheduler progress and increasing tail latency.
- Existing compatibility matrices live in design docs but are not represented by a small runtime contract that kernels, schedulers, and cache can implement with low coupling.

High-level approach:
Introduce a KV shim abstraction between the per-model KV cache and kernel execution. Responsibilities:
1) Encoded entry metadata: store lightweight tags with each KV chunk indicating encoding: INT8/GPTQ/AWQ/FP8/FP16, scale tables, and a small canonical checksum for deterministic replay.
2) Lazy dequantization API: kernels request KV slices with a desired execution precision and receive one of three modes:
   - QUANT_VIEW: read-only view of the quantized bytes (no copy, not writable) when the kernel supports on-the-fly quantized ops.
   - LAZY_DEQ: a transient dequantized view created on-demand, copy-on-write semantics; pinned until kernel completes. Backing storage can live on device or be CPU-paged depending on memory pressure and kernel hint.
   - EAGER_DEQ: full dequantized copy (backward-compatible mode).
3) Copy-on-write (COW) semantics: any kernel that mutates KV (rare for inference) will trigger a COW flow; kernels should be modified to signal non-mutating access where possible.
4) Epoch pinning and lightweight lease tokens: requests that hold LAZY_DEQ views receive a lease token; eviction honors tokens and will not reclaim pinned pages.

Encoding and metadata contract (fields attached to each KV chunk):
- encoding: one of {INT8, GPTQ, AWQ, FP8, FP16, FP32}
- scale_table_id: short id referencing quant tables (string)
- layout_hint: {contiguous, interleaved, packed-row}
- checksum: 64-bit hex string for determinism checks
- last_materialized_precision: last precision that produced a materialized dequantized blob (string)
These are small and should fit in the existing KV header region. Kernels must consult 'encoding' and 'layout_hint' before assuming byte layout.

Kernel constraints and recommendations:
- Kernel builders must expose a small capability query: supports_quant_view (boolean), supports_inplace_dequant (boolean), preferred_deq_mode (QUANT_VIEW, LAZY_DEQ, EAGER_DEQ). This can be an ABI-level flag exposed at model load time.
- Kernels that claim supports_quant_view must implement a tight path that operates directly on quantized bytes plus scale tables and must handle possible alignment differences indicated by layout_hint.
- For LAZY_DEQ, kernels must be tolerant of the backing buffer being CPU-pinned or device-resident; runtime will supply an address and a 'materialization_suggestion' (host_copy | gpu_pin) hint.
- Determinism: when kernel relies on dequantization, dequantization must follow an agreed algorithm (checksum verifies table used). If the quant-table id is missing, the runtime must reject LAZY_DEQ and fall back to EAGER_DEQ.

Scheduler interactions and policies:
- Scheduling unit must be precision-aware. When a request is scheduled it provides an 'execution_precision_hint' (soft): {min_acceptable, preferred, max_acceptable} to allow the scheduler to co-locate similar precision requests on same GPU or pick kernels that can avoid dequant copies.
- Coalescing window: the scheduler can delay tiny requests (<= 2 tokens) for a configurable microwindow (e.g., 0-1 ms) to allow quant-view reuse across requests (reduce materializations). This is opt-in per model route.
- Fallback: if a kernel declares it cannot satisfy the preferred mode, runtime tries progressively: QUANT_VIEW -> LAZY_DEQ -> EAGER_DEQ. Each step may be charged with a telemetry event.

Memory and eviction behavior:
- Entries have 'pin lease' counts; LAZY_DEQ increments pin until kernel releases token. Eviction will prefer "stale" quant encodings first (those with no materialized deq versions).
- Eviction policy extension: maintain hotness metrics at the encoding granularity (hot_quantized vs hot_materialized). This helps avoid thrashing by keeping quantized canonical copies while evicting expensive dequantized copies when memory is tight.
- Materialized dequant blobs should be tracked separately (secondary cache) and can be recycled if not used for N seconds (configurable).

Telemetry and safety signals:
- Emit events for: mode_chosen, materialization_time_ms, deq_memory_bytes, cache_hit_mode (quant_view|lazy_deq|eager_deq), checksum_mismatch.
- Add a sampling trace: on first few requests after model load or after quant-table update, force EAGER_DEQ and compare outputs to LAZY_DEQ/QUANT_VIEW for correctness/regression detection.

Determinism and validation tests:
- Unit tests: round-trip deq->compute->requant matches canonical eager path within tolerance thresholds; include seeds for RNG ops.
- Regression harness: add new evaluator that runs representative prompts across precision modes and asserts token-wise equality for deterministic models and bounded BLEU/ROUGE difference for non-deterministic sampling modes.
- CI job: nightly full-model quant-hash verification across all supported kernels and tables.

API/ABI changes (backwards compatible):
- At model load, the runtime will query model-specific kernel capabilities. Add a new optional capability block; older kernels that don't respond are assumed to only support EAGER_DEQ.
- KvManager: add get_kv_view(model_id, shard_id, token_range, mode_hint, lease_timeout_ms) -> {address, materialization_mode, lease_token}. Lease token is opaque string returned to caller and must be released.
- Release API: release_kv_lease(lease_token) – releases pins and allows eviction.
- These are additive and should not break existing pathways.

Safety and fallback matrix (quick):
- If checksum mismatch or missing scale table -> disallow QUANT_VIEW/LAZY_DEQ, force EAGER_DEQ and raise an alert.
- If memory pressure prevents LAZY_DEQ materialization on device, runtime will try CPU materialization (slower) then EAGER_DEQ.
- If any materialized deq is older than current model version -> invalidate and recompute.

Testing plan and rollout steps:
1) Feature branch with shim and modified test kernel that implements QUANT_VIEW. Unit tests only (no production).
2) Staging: enable for subset of non-critical models, enable telemetry and deterministic checks. Observe materialization rates and latency change.
3) Canary: enable for 10% of traffic on latency-sensitive routes using prefetched small prompts. Monitor tail latency, OOM signals, and checksum_mismatch.
4) Gradual ramp: if metrics stable, increase to 100% for models that benefit.
5) Hard off ramp: global kill switch and per-model disable for safety.

Developer notes and implementation hints:
- Prefer using GPU-side kernels that can operate on packed INT8 layout; this reduces need for LAZY_DEQ altogether for many workloads.
- For GPTQ/AWQ formats, keep quant tables immutable and reference-counted; small changes to tables should create new scale_table_id to avoid silent desync.
- Consider mmap-backed staged buffers for LAZY_DEQ to allow CPU fallback without reserializing.
- Keep the shim implementation minimal: the shim should not implement expensive dequant algorithms itself beyond a thin, optimized path; prefer shared library that kernels and runtime can call into.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is the optimal lease_timeout_ms default? 50ms? 200ms? Need perf runs.
- Is the checksum scheme (64-bit) sufficient to catch table mismatches? Should we include versioned table fingerprints delivered via model metadata?
- How to best expose coalescing window per-tenant without opening DOS vectors?
- Cost accounting: when LAZY_DEQ materializes on GPU, which tenant is billed and how to reflect in token-level cost?

Appendix: quick example: LAZY_DEQ flow for a 256-token prefix read:
1) Request arrives, scheduler picks kernel K which supports QUANT_VIEW and LAZY_DEQ preferred.
2) Runtime asks KV shim for QUANT_VIEW; shim returns zero-copy pointer to quant bytes and scale_table_id.
3) Kernel examines bytes and decides it can compute directly for first 128 tokens and requests LAZY_DEQ for tokens 129-256 as a contiguous range.
4) Shim materializes a device-resident LAZY_DEQ buffer for 129-256, returns lease_token.
5) Kernel completes, calls release_kv_lease(lease_token), shim decrements pin and updates hotness metrics.

Conclusion:
A small, well-scoped KV shim that provides QUANT_VIEW and LAZY_DEQ modes can significantly reduce memory traffic and tail latency for mixed-precision serving without requiring large kernel rewrites. The contract focuses on tiny metadata, lease tokens, and deterministic validation. If this proposal looks good, next step: prototype shim + one reference kernel (INT8 quant-view) and run microbenchmarks on a set of production-like prompts.

Checklist (next actions):
- [ ] Spike prototype: runtime + 1 kernel (Aisha)
- [ ] Add capability flags to kernel ABI (Miguel)
- [ ] CI regression harness for mode parity checks (Claire)
- [ ] Perf runs to tune lease_timeout and coalescing window (Daniel)

Notes to reviewers: this is a working draft. I'm intentionally keeping the shim small so adoption across models is incremental. Open to suggestions on the metadata schema and the telemetry fields.
